title: Slopulism is taking over America
gist: Noah Smith uses a proposed New York bill mandating a 10% self-checkout discount to argue that competitive grocery economics would invert the policy's intent and accelerate cashier replacement. He generalizes this into 'slopulism' — policies that look populist but cannot deliver what voters want — and warns it can become a bipartisan equilibrium when ideologues, not merely the ignorant, promote it.

insights.claim: New York Democrats have introduced a bill requiring grocery stores to give a 10% discount on all items purchased at self-checkout, justified on the grounds that customers scanning and bagging their own groceries are performing unpaid labor.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that anti-automation regulation is moving from rhetoric to legislative text in US retail.
insights.quote: New York Democrats introduce bill requiring 10% discounts on all items at self-checkout.
insights.locator: Would you like to see an example of a badly conceived policy?

insights.claim: Rhode Island was the first US state to enact statewide self-checkout restrictions, with its Restrictions on Self-Service Checkout Stations Act taking effect January 1, 2027 and requiring at least one human-operated checkout station for every three self-service stations during peak hours.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
entities: Restrictions on Self-Service Checkout Stations Act
insights.so_what: A hard staffing ratio written into state law raises grocery labor costs and caps the automation savings retailers can book in affected states.
insights.quote: The act requires grocery stores to have at least one human-operated checkout station for every three self-service stations during peak hours
insights.locator: Rhode Island was the first state in the U.S.

insights.claim: Similar self-checkout legislation has been introduced, enacted or considered in California, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Washington and Ohio, making retail anti-automation rules a multi-state trend rather than a local curiosity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk for grocery chains and self-checkout hardware vendors is spreading across large blue-state markets.
insights.quote: Similar legislation has either been introduced, enacted or considered in additional states including California, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Washington, and Ohio.
insights.locator: Rhode Island was the first state in the U.S.

insights.claim: Mandating a discount for self-checkout is economically identical to mandating a surcharge for using a human cashier, so the policy would cause grocery stores to fire cashiers and install more self-checkout machines — the exact opposite of its intended effect.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Price-wedge regulation on a substitute accelerates adoption of the substitute — the general failure mode to test before pricing any labor-protection rule.
insights.quote: forcing stores to charge more for purchases scanned by human cashiers will end up getting a lot of cashiers fired and replaced with self-checkout machines

insights.claim: Stores would fund a mandated self-checkout discount the way movie theaters fund senior and student discounts — by raising the sticker price so that post-discount prices leave overall revenue roughly unchanged — meaning the discount is nominal, not real.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Mandated discounts on a subset of transactions are absorbed by headline price increases, so consumer surplus does not rise — relevant to any price-mandate policy analysis.
insights.quote: You just raise the sticker price, so that the price people actually pay after the discount is the same as before.
insights.locator: But wait, you may be thinking

themes.theme: Grocery margin math forces the outcome

insights.claim: US grocery profit margins are almost always between 1.5% and 2.8%, very low compared with the average industry, which is why grocers cannot absorb a mandated self-checkout discount out of profits.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The thin-margin structure means any cost mandate on grocers passes through to shelf prices or headcount almost immediately.
insights.quote: Profit margins are almost always between 1.5% and 2.8%, which is very low compared to the average industry
insights.locator: Because the grocery store industry is very competitive

insights.claim: Because there are many grocery stores and new ones enter constantly, any chain that responded to the New York bill by dropping self-checkout to charge higher prices would be undercut by competitors offering self-checkout with big discounts, and would lose business until it installed the machines too.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Competitive entry — not regulator intent — determines the equilibrium; low barriers to entry make labor-protection mandates self-defeating.
insights.quote: other stores would undercut them by offering self-checkout with big discounts
insights.locator: It’s not just profit margins that demonstrate this

insights.claim: Forcing one substitute to cost more than another — like requiring stores to charge 10% more for Skippy than Jif peanut butter — pushes consumers to the cheaper option and results in less of the taxed good on the shelves, because in highly competitive industries consumers rather than retailers win.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A portable mental model for evaluating differential price mandates: identify the substitute, then assume the demand shifts fully toward it.
insights.quote: consumers tend to win out when an industry is highly competitive
insights.locator: This is kind of like if you told grocery stores

insights.claim: The honest version of the self-checkout debate is technocracy versus populism — protecting the livelihoods of a few cashiers against giving a huge number of consumers very slightly lower prices — and that tradeoff has no simple or easy conclusion.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Concedes that the standard efficiency argument does not settle automation politics — expect anti-automation policy to keep recurring even after each version is debunked.
insights.quote: protecting the livelihoods of a few cashiers versus giving a huge number of consumers very slightly lower prices
insights.locator: That argument is correct as far as it goes

insights.claim: 'Slopulism' is policy that looks like populism but would not achieve the results people want from it — snake oil that sells based on the public's inability to see the consequences of what it is being sold.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A screening label for policy risk: proposals that poll well but invert their own goals create regulatory whiplash rather than durable regimes.
insights.quote: It’s snake oil that sells well based on people’s inability to see the consequences of what they’re being sold.
insights.locator: The idea of a 10% discount on self-checkout

insights.claim: Slopulism is an inevitable outgrowth of populism: once people decide technocrats, elites, experts and gatekeepers aren't worth listening to, they become vulnerable to all sorts of policy scams.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Predicts a rising volume of economically incoherent legislation as anti-expert sentiment persists — a structural increase in policy uncertainty.
insights.quote: Once people decide that technocrats, elites, experts, and gatekeepers aren’t worth listening to, they become vulnerable to all sorts of policy scams.
insights.locator: Slopulism is an inevitable outgrowth of populism

insights.claim: Policy scams split into accidental ones, where policymakers simply don't understand what they're doing, and ideological ones, where ideologues sell the public a policy by pretending it offers benefits it doesn't — and the ideological variety is the more dangerous.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Diagnostic for how persistent a bad policy will be: ignorance is correctable by evidence, deliberate misdirection is not.
insights.locator: In general, these scams fall into two categories

insights.claim: Social media makes accidental slopulism harder to correct because it elevates the dumbest and loudest voices at the expense of the most well-informed, though patience, education, reason — and possibly AI — can still overcome it.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Positions AI as a countervailing force to information-environment degradation — an underrated civic use case beyond productivity.
insights.quote: social media — which elevates the dumbest and loudest at the expense of the most well-informed — probably makes it harder
insights.locator: Slopulism that arises out of pure ignorance

insights.claim: The danger is that slopulism becomes a bipartisan equilibrium, with each party's ideologues executing a coup against reasonable moderates by appealing to slopulist instincts.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: If both parties converge on economically incoherent policy, election outcomes stop hedging regulatory risk for businesses.
insights.quote: there’s the danger that slopulism becomes a bipartisan equilibrium, with each party’s ideologues executing a coup against the reasonable moderates by appealing to slopulist instincts
insights.locator: But when slopulist ideas are being promoted by smart people

insights.claim: The self-checkout analysis is undergraduate-level microeconomics that any economist or any good AI would reproduce, yet public responses on X showed widespread inability to follow it — evidence that the constraint on good policy is comprehension, not analytical difficulty.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The bottleneck on policy quality is public economic literacy, which sets a low ceiling on how technocratic reforms can be sold.
insights.quote: If you ask any economist, or any good AI, they’ll give basically the same answer, in different words.
insights.locator: As policies go, this example isn’t particularly hard to explain
